title: Even when roughly 20% of the film was never finished, On the Silver Globe still provides more food for thought than most other films.

commenti.body:
I'm in the minority here but I found most of the psychbabble in this movie empty nothing. It was just endless talking and they're mostly all insane saying nothing of interest. I thought the need to have them speak in psychobabble really undermined the more interesting questions raised by the story, some of which you highlight.  It also didn't help that the Earth scenes were so under-developed at the end.

I'm not sure the missing parts matter much. They seem to be largely plot scenes.

I can understand that, in the end it depends on the viewers preference. For me personally, the philosophical talk was fitting for the film. The astronauts entered another planet and were alone. I think this is something that has a lot of impact on the mind and sanity of a person. I'd like to think the philosphical talk was due to them having a lot of time with their own thoughts.

That’s a good explanation. I found the first hour the least off putting. But also it’s a remarkable production well worth celebrating. It’s not a movie I loved but I love that it exists if that makes sense. I just think stuff like Stalker works the same field with more thoughtful ideas.
That does make sense! And yeah, I agree that Stalker is philosophically more interesting

I posted about this film a week or so ago, and you've verbalised some of the thoughts I had about it that I didn't really articulate. It was amazing seeing the natural emergence of religion, mythology, superstition, etc... And like you say, these are all things that are baked into the human condition when they find themselves trying to make sense of their environment.

On a completely different note: did you notice how each of the three colonized planets - Earth, New Earth, and the middle planet where the two guys watch the video of the first astronauts, all had those same tribal guys in the furs and whatnot? 

It seemed to me to be shorthand for saying that just as the tribal origins/nature of mankind are inevitable, so too is the descent back into tribalism.

I'm a big fan of Stalker... But I'm surprised to hear you say you found it more philosophically interesting. On the Silver Globe touches on so many different questions... If you get a moment, could you tell me why you find Stalker more philosophically interesting?

I wasn't even aware there was a middle planet! I thought the 2 guys were on Old Earth...

>It seemed to me to be shorthand for saying that just as the tribal origins/nature of mankind are inevitable, so too is the descent back into tribalism.

This is very interesting!

On the Silver Globe had a lot more philosophical questions which are also very interesting, but for me what made Stalker more interesting is the question whether we know what we desire most. And even if we think we know what we desire most, how are we so sure? Also the different aspects from Stalker, Professor and Writer in the Zone are interesting

I think the two films take two radically different approaches. 

On the Silver Globe lays it all out there for you to experience, whereas Stalker leaves almost every aspect unseen and unsaid. It makes for a more mysterious, introspective experience.
Definitely! It leaves the door open for your own interpretations.
I could be wrong about there being a third planet. That's just the impression I got. However, it would also fit if it was just Earth, since that had tribals too.
Do you often ponder on existential questions in your day to day life?
Yes but not ranting and raving like a first year psych textbook, which was my issue here. No one actually talks about things they just philosophize.

If you ask me it's pretty apt, the main character is an astronaut who's literally gone insane, he's a messiah who gets cheated on with an infernal bird creature. It's more shakespeare play than it is psych textbook.

And more interesting than that, the film itself is insanity, there is a blurring of reality and fiction in that some of the things the crew had to go through to bring to life the vision of the director are quite intense.
